# Navapur — implemented workshop script

The following supplied draft replaces the earlier seven-scene storyboard. Final overall timings remain provisional.

Navapur — script, first draft
Working draft implemented in this experience.

Materials: sticky notes or paper, pens, printed solution sheets. No wall needed. Everything happens on the tables. A facilitator can record results in a spreadsheet as the session goes.

The idea
The workshop is the way Civic Games Lab works, run in an hour. We don't play anyone. We understand people's motivations and needs, and we let their voices shape how the game is designed. Our job is to build the simulation. The people who live inside it are the ones who make the decisions.

Inside the simulation, people enter the system, make choices, see the game state change, test again, and go round once more. Along the way they build a vocabulary for what they want to do and what their future should look like. That vocabulary turns into projects, and we keep the process going.

Each section of the workshop is one step of that loop, done through its own exercise.

Workshop section	Step in the process	Exercise in the room
1. Navapur	Understand the place	The story, in chapters
2. Who are you?	Understand the people	Pick a role and a motivation, then tell your table
3. Peak	Imagine the future	Peak phone, tyres, travel and clothes
4. What's the problem?	Name the problems	One problem each, three per table, a vote, then the problem in the short, medium and long term
5. Solutions	Build a vocabulary	The peak solution, then Action (short term), Best Practice (medium term), Innovation (long term)
6. Force majeure	See the state change	One shock; the room responds
7. Climate manifesto	Enter the system and choose	The room writes one climate manifesto for the year and spends ₹10 crore
8. What we tried to do today	Projects, and keep going	Summary
1 · Navapur
One image throughout. The drought image comes in at chapter 5 and the flood image at chapter 6. One chapter per click.

Chapter 1 — The capital
For most of its history, Navapur was a market town. Farmers from the surrounding villages brought their cotton to the mandi, sold it and went home the same day. A few years ago the state created a new district and made Navapur its capital. Government offices, banks and schools followed, and people came from across the region to work and build. About fifty thousand people live here now, and more arrive every year.

Chapter 2 — Cotton
Navapur is known as the cotton capital of India, and the town still runs on it. From October to December, trolleys of cotton line up outside the mandi and the ginning mills work through the night. Most families here earn something from cotton, whether they grow it, pick it, transport it, gin it, trade it or lend money against it.

Chapter 3 — Growth
Navapur is expanding quickly into the farmland around it. Each year more fields are sold and turned into housing colonies, shops, warehouses and petrol pumps. Villages that were a short drive away are now part of the town's edge. Some farmers have sold their land and invested in the town. Others still farm, now alongside new roads and buildings.

Chapter 4 — From panchayat to municipality
As the town spreads, the way it is governed is changing too. Villages around Navapur that were run by their own gram panchayats are being brought inside the municipal boundary. The sarpanch and the gram sabha are giving way to ward councillors and municipal officers. Property tax, building permissions, water connections and waste collection are now meant to come from the town. But the new system is still being set up, and people in the new wards are not always sure who to go to, or whether anyone will come.

Chapter 5 — Water
Navapur depends on groundwater, and the water table is falling. Farms, mills and new colonies all draw from the same aquifer, and most of them dig their own borewells. Each year the wells have to go deeper. In some parts of town they now run dry by March, and families buy water from tankers until the monsoon. How much water is drawn, and how much is left, is not yet measured or managed together.

Chapter 6 — Heat, waste and floods
Summers are hotter than they used to be. In May there are weeks above 45°C, outdoor work stops by late morning, and when the whole town turns on its coolers at once the power fails. The town produces more waste each year than it collects, and much of it ends up in open plots and drains. So when the monsoon arrives, often late and then heavy, the blocked drains push water back into the lanes and the old town around the pond floods first. In the fields, cotton that was nearly ready to pick is damaged before it can be harvested.

Chapter 7 — The budget
This year Navapur has ₹10 crore to spend. Farmers, traders, builders, officials and residents all have their own idea of what it should be spent on. Today you'll decide.

The solution sheet has three rows, one per round. Each matches a horizon from screen 4.4.

Round 1

Action · short term What can Navapur do this year with what it already has?

Round 2

Best Practice · medium term What has worked somewhere else that Navapur could adapt within five years?

Round 3

Innovation · long term What would have to exist in ten years that doesn't exist today?

Each round shows the current step and its timer:

Talk 1:30 · Write 1:30 · Pass · Improve 1:00

6 · Force majeure
The facilitator picks one shock. The other two stay prepared but are not shown.

Screen 6.1: The shock

Force majeure

Then one of these:

A week above 47°C. Power demand jumps and the grid fails for hours at a time. Outdoor work stops. Borewells run dry in April.

The monsoon is three weeks late. Then it rains for three days. The old town floods. Fields are waterlogged. The main road to the mandi is closed.

The price of cotton falls by a third. Farmers can't repay their crop loans. The ginning mills cut their shifts. Shops lose their busiest season.

7 · Climate manifesto

10:00

8 · What we tried to do today
What we tried to do today

We started with a place, and the people who live in it. We tried to understand what they want and what they need. We built a simulation of Navapur so they could make decisions inside it. You named the problems, and chose which ones come first. You imagined the final version of a solution, and worked back from it. You found words for what Navapur could do, and what it could become. A shock came, and you responded. Then you wrote a climate manifesto for the year and spent the budget.

That's how projects begin.

We keep the process going.
